chunks.text: Tabebuia rosea, known as the pink trumpet tree, pink poui or rosy trumpet tree, is a neotropical Bignoniaceae species native from southern Mexico to Venezuela and Ecuador, growing up to about 30 m with an irregular, layered branching habit and a trunk to 1 m in diameter. Its palmately compound leaves are shed during the dry season, when the tree produces its signature large pink-to-purple flowers, mainly in January and February, followed by slender wind-dispersed seed capsules up to 35 cm long. It is the national tree of El Salvador, where it is called maquilíshuat, and in Malaysia — where it is an introduced but well-adapted ornamental — its seasonal pink bloom has earned it the local nickname 'Malaysia Sakura' for its resemblance to cherry blossom. Traditional medicine uses bark, flowers, leaves and roots against intestinal parasites, malaria, anaemia, constipation and fever; its main bioactive compound, the naphthoquinone lapachol, was investigated as a cancer treatment but is now considered too toxic for that purpose, though it does show antimalarial activity. Its wood resembles oak (hence the Costa Rican name 'roble de sabana', savannah oak), and its flowers attract both insect and bird pollinators, including tanagers, hummingbirds and orioles; the tree is also noted for persisting in heavily deforested landscapes thanks to its easily wind-dispersed, readily germinating seed.

This horticultural reference describes Tabebuia rosea as a deciduous tree with a rounded crown and a straight, often buttressed bole up to a metre across, flowering while leafless in shades from deep rose-purple to, occasionally, white. It ranges naturally from northern South America (Ecuador, Colombia, Venezuela) through the Caribbean and Central America to Mexico, growing in moist or fairly dry forest, open fields and along roadsides up to about 1,200 m in Guatemala, and tolerating annual rainfall from 1,250 to 2,500 mm and temperatures from 17 to 34°C. Unlike many ornamental trees, it carries real economic weight as one of Central America's most important timber species: its greyish-brown, finely striped wood is moderately hard, durable and easy to work, and is used in heavy construction, furniture, interior finish, boatbuilding and carts, with a large share of the region's cheaper chairs made from it. It also serves as a shade tree in coffee and cocoa agroforestry systems. The database notes it has some weed potential and can become locally invasive, but lists no known edible or medicinal uses — a useful corrective to looser claims elsewhere, since the IUCN (2019) otherwise rates it a secure species of Least Concern with a wide range and no major identified threats.
